semantic_correction.stem: A community health nurse is teaching adults who receive take-home naloxone kits. Which statement by a participant shows correct understanding of how to respond to a suspected opioid overdose?

options.A: If I suspect an opioid overdose, I can give naloxone, call 911, support breathing as able, place the person on the side, and stay until help arrives.
options.B: If the person wakes after naloxone, I can continue watching at home and call 911 later if slowed breathing or unresponsiveness develops again.
options.C: I can give naloxone before opioid use when overdose risk seems high, then monitor closely and repeat a dose if signs of opioid overdose later appear.
options.D: I should call 911 and keep the person on the side, but wait for a health professional to administer naloxone because emergency medication requires training.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC guidance states that when an overdose is suspected, a bystander can administer naloxone if available and call 911, try to keep the person awake and breathing, place the person on the side to reduce choking risk, and stay until emergency assistance arrives. CDC also states that anyone can carry and administer naloxone and that naloxone cannot be taken before drug use to prevent an overdose. Therefore A shows correct understanding. B incorrectly treats awakening after naloxone as a reason to delay emergency activation. C incorrectly describes naloxone as prophylaxis before opioid use. D includes useful supportive actions but incorrectly delays naloxone for a health professional even though CDC explicitly supports bystander administration.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach community members to administer naloxone promptly for a suspected opioid overdose as part of an emergency response that also includes calling 911, supporting breathing, positioning to reduce choking risk, and staying with the person until help arrives.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: What to Do If You Think Someone Is Overdosing; Naloxone Frequently Asked Questions; Lifesaving Naloxone
semantic_correction.source_version_date: CDC overdose-response resources dated 2024–2025 and live/rechecked August 20, 2026; current 2026 CDC fentanyl-awareness material independently continues to state that anyone can carry naloxone
semantic_correction.source_locator: What to Do If You Think Someone Is Overdosing, ‘Steps to take’: administer naloxone if available and call 911; try to keep the person awake and breathing; lay the person on the side to prevent choking; stay until emergency assistance arrives. Naloxone FAQ: anyone can carry/administer naloxone and it cannot be taken prior to drug use to prevent an overdose. Lifesaving Naloxone: anyone can carry and give naloxone to someone experiencing an overdose.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Community members can administer naloxone for a suspected opioid overdose and should pair it with emergency activation and supportive care while staying with the person; naloxone is not a pre-use preventive medication.
semantic_correction.blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
semantic_correction.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance, printed p.9 (official PDF pageno 12): plan and/or participate in community health education; educate client about prevention and treatment of high-risk health behaviors; assess and educate clients about health risks based on family, population and community.
semantic_correction.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — community opioid-overdose prevention and take-home naloxone education
semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup retained the take-home-naloxone construct, removed the absolute-word distractor pattern, balanced A/B/C/D length, and made the key a complete CDC-supported bystander overdose response rather than a uniquely verbose option.

scope_exclusions.dose_timing: No numeric naloxone redosing interval or dose count is tested.
scope_exclusions.route: No specific naloxone product, nasal-spray strength, injection route, or device technique is tested.
scope_exclusions.legal_protection: No state-specific Good Samaritan law or immunity claim is tested.
scope_exclusions.observation_duration: No fixed post-naloxone observation duration is tested; the item uses the CDC action of staying until emergency assistance arrives.
scope_exclusions.etiology: The item is limited to suspected opioid overdose and does not claim naloxone reverses non-opioid toxicity.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for ‘naloxone suspected opioid overdose call 911 stay with person bystander take-home kit’ returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank scan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It integrates naloxone administration with emergency activation, breathing support, recovery positioning, and continued presence until help arrives.
option_audit.B: Plausible because naloxone can produce rapid clinical improvement, but emergency assistance should not be deferred merely because the person awakens.
option_audit.C: Plausible to a learner who thinks of naloxone as prevention, but CDC explicitly states it cannot be taken in advance to prevent an overdose.
option_audit.D: Plausible because calling 911 and side positioning are appropriate, but CDC supports bystander naloxone administration without waiting for a health professional.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A alone contains the recommended bystander naloxone response without delaying emergency care, misusing naloxone prophylactically, or reserving administration for professionals.

cueing_check.note: The key is not longest; all alternatives are first-person participant statements of comparable length and clinical detail.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: NCSBN explicitly includes community health education and education about prevention/treatment of high-risk health behaviors; take-home naloxone teaching directly maps to these entry-level RN activities.
blueprint_audit.visual_verification: VERIFIED. Official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan screenshot pageno 12 / printed p.9 was successfully retrieved August 20, 2026 and visibly shows the cited Health Promotion and Maintenance activity statements.

source_verification.note: Multiple live CDC overdose-prevention pages were rechecked August 20, 2026. A current 2026 CDC toolkit independently confirms that naloxone remains a bystander-usable opioid-overdose reversal medication.
